chapters.n: Zechariah began prophesying in late 520 BC, just two months after Haggai, to the Jews rebuilding the temple. He was from a priestly family that returned from Babylon.

f.g: His name means “Jehovah remembers.”

chapters.n: The Lord was very angry with their ancestors, whose sins led to Jerusalem’s destruction and exile.

f.g: Extremely angry.

chapters.n: The key invitation of the book: “Turn to Me, and I will turn to you.” God is ready to meet anyone who comes back to Him.

f.w: Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you

chapters.n: Don’t be like your ancestors who ignored the earlier prophets’ calls to repent.

f.g: Prophets before the exile, such as Isaiah and Jeremiah.

f.w: Turn ye now from your evil ways

chapters.n: Where are your ancestors now? And the prophets — they didn’t live forever either. People pass away; God’s word remains.
God’s words caught up with their ancestors, who finally admitted, “The Lord dealt with us just as our ways deserved.” Prophecy proves true.

f.g: Overtake — like a pursuer catching up.

chapters.n: Three months later (February 519 BC), Zechariah receives a series of eight night visions.

f.g: Shebat, the eleventh month (January–February).

chapters.n: Vision one: a man on a red horse stands among myrtle trees in a hollow, with red, sorrel, and white horses behind him.

f.g: Fragrant evergreen shrubs; later a symbol of Israel’s restoration (Isaiah 55:13).
Probably sorrel or reddish-brown.

chapters.n: Zechariah asks what they mean. An interpreting angel promises to explain — a pattern throughout these visions.

f.w: the angel that talked with me
f.g: A guiding angel who explains each vision.

chapters.n: The rider explains: these are the Lord’s scouts, sent to patrol the earth.

f.w: walk to and fro through the earth

chapters.n: The patrol reports to the angel of the Lord: the whole earth is calm and at rest. The Persian Empire was at peace — yet Jerusalem remained in ruins.

f.g: A heavenly messenger who speaks with God’s authority.

chapters.n: The angel of the Lord intercedes: “How long, Lord, before You show mercy to Jerusalem? You’ve been angry for seventy years.” Heaven itself pleads for God’s people.
The Lord replies with kind and comforting words.

f.g: Comforting words.

chapters.n: The message to proclaim: the Lord is deeply, passionately devoted to Jerusalem and Zion.
God is angry with nations that feel secure. He was only a little angry with His people, but those nations went too far in hurting them.

f.g: They made the punishment worse than God intended.

f.w: I was but a little displeased

chapters.n: The Lord has returned to Jerusalem with mercy. His temple will be rebuilt and the city measured out again for rebuilding.

f.w: my house shall be built in it
a line shall be stretched forth
f.g: A measuring line — a sign of planned rebuilding.

chapters.n: God’s cities will overflow with prosperity again. He will comfort Zion and choose Jerusalem.

f.w: the LORD shall yet comfort Zion

chapters.n: Vision two: Zechariah sees four horns. In scripture, horns symbolize power, especially of kings and nations.

f.g: Four could represent the four directions — every power from all sides.

chapters.n: The angel explains: these horns are the powers that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.
Then the Lord shows four craftsmen.

f.g: Craftsmen or smiths — workers skilled in shaping and breaking.

chapters.n: The craftsmen have come to terrify and cut down the horns. For every power that harms God’s people, God has an answer.

f.g: Frighten, terrify.

f.w: cast out the horns of the Gentiles

chapters.n: Vision three: a man with a measuring line in his hand.
He is going to measure Jerusalem’s width and length — perhaps to plan its walls.
The interpreting angel goes out, and another angel comes to meet him.

f.g: A second heavenly messenger with urgent news.

chapters.n: “Run, tell that young man: Jerusalem will be like an unwalled town because of all its people and animals.” The city will grow beyond any wall.

f.g: Open villages — so crowded no wall could contain them.
Probably the man with the measuring line — or Zechariah himself.

chapters.n: God Himself will be a wall of fire around Jerusalem and the glory within it. His presence is better protection than stone.

f.w: the glory in the midst of her

chapters.n: “Come out! Flee from the north country!” Many Jews still lived in Babylon (north by the travel route). God calls the scattered to come home.

f.g: An urgent call — “Hurry!”

chapters.n: Escape, Zion, you who live with Babylon! A call to leave behind the world and come to God’s city — echoed in latter-day revelation.
Whoever touches God’s people touches the apple of His eye — the pupil, the most sensitive part. God feels harm done to His people as harm done to Himself.

f.g: The pupil — something precious and fiercely protected.

f.w: he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of his eye

chapters.n: God will wave His hand against the oppressors, and they will be plundered by their former slaves. Then you’ll know the Lord sent this messenger.

f.g: A threatening gesture.

chapters.n: Sing and rejoice, Zion! The Lord says, “I am coming, and I will live among you.” Christians hear in this the promise of Christ dwelling among His people.

f.w: Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion
I will dwell in the midst of thee

chapters.n: Many nations will join themselves to the Lord and become His people. The gospel is for all.

f.w: many nations shall be joined to the LORD

chapters.n: The Lord will claim Judah as His special portion in the holy land and choose Jerusalem again. This is the only place in the Bible where the phrase “holy land” appears.

f.g: The only use of this exact phrase in the Bible.

chapters.n: Let all humanity be silent before the Lord, for He is rising from His holy dwelling to act.

f.w: Be silent, O all flesh, before the LORD

chapters.n: Vision four: a heavenly courtroom. Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the Lord, and Satan (“the accuser”) stands ready to accuse him.

f.g: Hebrew ha-satan, “the adversary” or “accuser.”

chapters.n: The Lord rebukes the accuser. Isn’t Joshua a burning stick snatched from the fire — rescued from exile? God defends those He has saved.

f.w: a brand plucked out of the fire

chapters.n: Joshua stands dressed in filthy clothes — representing his sin and the sin of the people he represents.

f.g: Hebrew suggests clothing soiled with excrement — the vilest uncleanness.

chapters.n: The angel orders the filthy clothes removed: “I have taken away your sin and will clothe you in fine garments.” A powerful image of forgiveness through the Savior’s Atonement.

f.w: I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee

f.g: Festal or rich garments.

chapters.n: Zechariah himself speaks up: “Put a clean turban on his head!” Joshua is fully restored to priestly service.

f.g: The high priest’s turban, which bore the words “Holiness to the Lord” (Exodus 28:36-38).

chapters.n: The angel of the Lord then solemnly charges Joshua.

f.g: Solemnly declared or charged.

chapters.n: If Joshua walks in God’s ways and keeps His charge, he will govern God’s house and courts and have access among those standing in God’s presence. Forgiveness invites faithful service.

f.w: places to walk among these that stand by
f.g: Access to God’s presence, among the angels who serve Him.

chapters.n: Joshua and his fellow priests are a sign of something to come: God will bring His servant, the Branch — a title of the Messiah from David’s line.

f.g: Men who are a sign or omen.

chapters.n: A stone with seven eyes is set before Joshua. God will engrave it and remove the land’s sin in a single day — many Christians see this fulfilled in Christ’s atoning sacrifice.
In that day everyone will invite neighbors to sit under their vine and fig tree — a picture of peace and security.

f.w: under the vine and under the fig tree

chapters.n: The angel returns and rouses Zechariah as though from sleep, preparing him for vision five.

f.g: Roused him to full spiritual alertness.

chapters.n: He sees a golden lampstand with a bowl on top feeding seven lamps through pipes.

f.g: A lampstand (menorah), like the one in the tabernacle.

chapters.n: Two olive trees stand beside it, one on each side, supplying oil.
Zechariah asks what these things mean.

f.g: Zechariah models humble questioning.

chapters.n: The angel asks if he understands; Zechariah honestly admits he doesn’t.

f.g: Humility opens the way for revelation.

chapters.n: The key message for Zerubbabel: the temple will be finished “not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.” Just as the lamp burns with a steady oil supply, God’s work goes forward by His Spirit.

f.w: Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit

chapters.n: Every mountain-sized obstacle will become flat ground before Zerubbabel. He will set the final stone amid shouts of “Grace, grace to it!”

f.g: The top or capstone — the final stone marking completion.
A shout of blessing: “How beautiful!”

chapters.n: Another word from the Lord comes to Zechariah.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: A formula introducing a new revelation.

chapters.n: Zerubbabel laid the temple foundation, and he will finish it. It was completed in 515 BC.

f.w: his hands shall also finish it

chapters.n: Don’t despise small beginnings! People will rejoice to see Zerubbabel holding the plumb line. The “seven” are the Lord’s eyes that see everything on earth.

f.w: who hath despised the day of small things?

f.g: Plumb line, or a special “tin stone” — a builder’s tool.

f.w: the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro

chapters.n: Zechariah asks about the two olive trees.

f.w: What are these two olive trees

chapters.n: He asks more specifically about two olive branches that pour golden oil through golden pipes.

f.g: Literally “the gold” — the gleaming olive oil.

chapters.n: Again the angel asks; again Zechariah admits he doesn’t know.

f.w: Knowest thou not what these be?
f.g: The repeated question deepens the anticipation.

chapters.n: They are “the two anointed ones” who stand by the Lord of all the earth — likely Zerubbabel (the royal leader) and Joshua (the high priest). Revelation uses the same image for two latter-day witnesses.

f.g: Literally “sons of oil” — the governor and the priest, both anointed to serve.

f.w: that stand by the Lord of the whole earth

chapters.n: Vision six: a flying scroll soaring through the air.

f.g: A scroll.

chapters.n: The scroll is huge — about 30 by 15 feet (9 by 4.5 meters), the same size as the porch of Solomon’s temple. It is unrolled so all can read it.

f.g: A cubit is about 18 inches (45 cm); so about 30 feet long.

chapters.n: The scroll is a curse going out over the land against thieves on one side and those who swear falsely on the other — sins against neighbor and against God.

f.g: Swears falsely — perjury, taking God’s name in vain.

chapters.n: God sends the curse into the homes of thieves and perjurers, where it stays and destroys even timber and stone. Sin eats away at a household from within.

f.w: him that sweareth falsely by my name

chapters.n: The angel tells Zechariah to look at something else coming out — vision seven.

f.g: Comes out, appears.

chapters.n: It is an ephah — a large measuring basket. It represents the sin of people throughout the land.

f.g: A measuring basket holding about 5 gallons (20 liters).
Appearance — or, in some versions, “their iniquity.”

chapters.n: A heavy lead lid is lifted, revealing a woman sitting inside the basket.

f.g: A round lead cover weighing about 75 pounds (34 kg).

chapters.n: The angel says, “This is Wickedness,” and shoves her back into the basket, slamming the lead lid shut. Evil is contained.
Two women with stork-like wings, carried by the wind, lift the basket into the sky.

f.g: A large migrating bird with a wide wingspan — ironically an unclean bird in the law of Moses.

chapters.n: Zechariah asks where they are taking it.

f.w: Whither do these bear the ephah?
f.g: Where is the sin being taken?

chapters.n: To Shinar (Babylonia), where a house will be built for it. Wickedness is removed from the holy land and sent back to Babylon — the symbol of worldliness.

f.w: set there upon her own base
f.g: Placed on a pedestal — like an idol in a temple.

chapters.n: The eighth and final vision: four chariots coming out between two bronze mountains — perhaps the gateway of heaven.

f.g: Bronze — strong and unbreakable.

chapters.n: The first chariot has red horses, the second black.
The third has white horses, the fourth dappled ones.

f.g: Dappled and strong (or spotted).

chapters.n: Zechariah asks what they are.
They are the four spirits (or winds) of heaven, going out after standing before the Lord of all the earth — His agents carrying out His will everywhere.

f.w: the four spirits of the heavens
f.g: Hebrew ruḥot can mean “winds” or “spirits.”

chapters.n: The black horses head north, with the white following; the dappled head south.

f.g: Babylon and Mesopotamia — reached from Israel by a northern route.

chapters.n: The strong horses are eager to go throughout the earth, and they are sent to patrol it.

f.w: walk to and fro through the earth

chapters.n: The Lord says those going north have given His Spirit rest there — His judgment on Babylon is accomplished.

f.g: Settled My anger — satisfied My justice.

chapters.n: After the visions, a new message from the Lord comes with a symbolic action.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me

chapters.n: Zechariah is to receive gifts from three returned exiles — Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah — and go to Josiah’s house.

f.g: Exiles who had returned from Babylon, bringing donations.

chapters.n: With the silver and gold he is to make crowns and place one on Joshua the high priest’s head — a surprising act, since crowns belonged to kings, not priests.

f.g: Hebrew plural, perhaps an ornate crown with several circlets.

chapters.n: “Behold the man whose name is the Branch.” He will grow up from his place and build the Lord’s temple. The Branch is a messianic title; Pilate’s words “Behold the man!” echo this phrase.
The Branch will build the temple, bear royal glory, and rule as both king and priest on his throne — two roles united. Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus, our King and High Priest.

f.w: he shall be a priest upon his throne
the counsel of peace shall be between them both
f.g: Harmony between the royal and priestly offices.

chapters.n: The crown will be kept in the temple as a memorial honoring the donors.

f.g: Apparently another name for Heldai (v. 10).
“Grace” — perhaps a title for Josiah (v. 10).

chapters.n: People from far away will come help build the temple. This will happen — if they diligently obey the Lord. God’s promises are tied to obedience.

f.w: they that are far off shall come

chapters.n: Two years later (December 518 BC), a new message comes. The temple was about halfway finished.

f.g: Kislev, the ninth month (November–December).

chapters.n: People from Bethel send a delegation to seek the Lord at the temple.

f.g: Leaders of the delegation; their Babylonian-style names show exile’s influence.

chapters.n: Their question: “Should we keep mourning and fasting in the fifth month, as we have for so many years?” They had fasted yearly to remember the temple’s destruction. Now that it was being rebuilt, was it still needed?
The Lord answers through Zechariah — but not right away with a yes or no.

f.w: the word of the LORD of hosts
f.g: God’s answer goes deeper than the question.

chapters.n: When you fasted all those seventy years, was it really for Me? God asks them to examine their motives.

f.g: The seventh-month fast recalled the murder of governor Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:25).

f.w: did ye at all fast unto me

chapters.n: And when you ate and drank at feasts, wasn’t that for yourselves too? Religious practices can become self-centered.

f.w: did not ye eat for yourselves

chapters.n: Isn’t this the same message the earlier prophets gave when Jerusalem was prosperous and the land was full of people? The answer was already given before the exile.

f.g: The Negev (southern desert) and the Shephelah (foothills).

chapters.n: Zechariah restates the earlier prophets’ core message.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto Zechariah
f.g: Introducing a summary of the prophets’ message.

chapters.n: Judge with true justice; show kindness and compassion to each other. This matters more to God than rituals.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant kindness.

chapters.n: Don’t oppress widows, orphans, foreigners, or the poor, and don’t even plot evil against one another in your hearts. God cares about the vulnerable.

f.w: oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless

chapters.n: But their ancestors refused to listen. Like a stubborn ox, they jerked their shoulder away and plugged their ears.

f.g: Like an ox refusing the yoke.

chapters.n: They made their hearts hard as flint to avoid hearing God’s law and the words His Spirit spoke through the prophets. So great anger came.

f.g: Diamond or flint — extremely hard.

f.w: they made their hearts as an adamant stone

chapters.n: Because they wouldn’t listen when God called, God wouldn’t listen when they called.

f.w: they cried, and I would not hear

chapters.n: So God scattered them like a whirlwind among unknown nations, and the beautiful land became desolate. Their own choices ruined “the pleasant land.”

f.w: I scattered them with a whirlwind

chapters.n: A new series of ten promises begins, each opening “Thus saith the Lord of hosts.”

f.w: the word of the LORD of hosts
f.g: Zechariah 8 contains ten short oracles of hope.

chapters.n: God is fiercely devoted to Zion, burning with zeal to protect her.
The Lord has returned and will live in Jerusalem. It will be called the City of Truth (Faithfulness), and His mountain the Holy Mountain.

f.g: Or “the faithful city.”

chapters.n: Elderly men and women will again sit in Jerusalem’s streets, leaning on canes — a sign of long, peaceful lives.
The streets will be full of boys and girls playing. Few images of peace are more beautiful than safe, happy children.
This may seem too wonderful to the struggling remnant, but is it too hard for God? Nothing is impossible with Him.

f.w: should it also be marvellous in mine eyes?

chapters.n: God will rescue His people from east and west — from everywhere.

f.w: from the east country, and from the west country

chapters.n: They will live in Jerusalem and be His people, and He will be their God in faithfulness and righteousness — the heart of the covenant.

f.w: they shall be my people, and I will be their God

chapters.n: Let your hands be strong, you who heard the prophets when the temple foundation was laid. Keep building!
Before the work began, there were no wages, no profit for man or beast, and no safety — everyone was against everyone.

f.w: there was no hire for man

chapters.n: But now God will treat this remnant differently than before.

f.g: The remnant who returned.

chapters.n: Seed will prosper, vines bear fruit, the ground yield crops, and the sky give dew. God will give all this to the remnant.

f.w: the heavens shall give their dew

chapters.n: Judah and Israel had been a byword for a curse among nations; now God will save them, and they will be a blessing. Don’t fear — be strong.
Just as God determined to punish their ancestors and did not relent…

f.g: I did not relent or change My mind.

chapters.n: …so now He is determined to do good to Jerusalem and Judah. Don’t be afraid. God’s determination to bless is as firm as His justice.
Here is what you must do: speak truth to one another and give true, peaceful verdicts in your courts.

f.w: Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour

f.g: The city gates, where courts met.

chapters.n: Don’t plot evil against your neighbor, and don’t love false oaths — God hates these things.

f.w: all these are things that I hate

chapters.n: Another word from the Lord — now He finally answers the question about fasting from chapter 7.

f.w: the word of the LORD of hosts came unto me

chapters.n: The four fasts mourning Jerusalem’s fall will become joyful feasts. Sorrow will turn to gladness. So love truth and peace.

f.w: The fast of the fourth month

chapters.n: People from many cities will come.
People from one city will urge others: “Let’s go at once to pray to the Lord! I’m going too.” Faith spreads by invitation.
Many peoples and powerful nations will come to Jerusalem to seek and pray to the Lord.

f.w: many people and strong nations shall come

chapters.n: Ten people from every language will grab the robe of one Jew and say, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.” Israel will become a light drawing the world to God.

f.g: A full number — many people.
The hem or fringe (tassel) of the robe, a sign of covenant (Numbers 15:38-39).

chapters.n: The second part of Zechariah (chapters 9–14) looks further ahead, especially to the Messiah. It opens with judgment on Israel’s northern neighbors in Syria — everyone, Israel included, will look to the Lord.

f.g: A weighty prophetic oracle.
A region in northern Syria, known from Assyrian records.

chapters.n: Hamath, also in Syria, and the proud Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon, famous for their cleverness, are included.
Tyre built itself an island fortress and piled up silver and gold like dust and mud. Wealth bred false security.

f.g: Tyre was an island city with massive walls — a pun, since “stronghold” (matsor) sounds like “Tyre” (Tsor).

chapters.n: But the Lord will strip Tyre, destroy its sea power, and burn it. Alexander the Great famously captured island Tyre in 332 BC.

f.w: she shall be devoured with fire

chapters.n: The Philistine cities — Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron — will watch Tyre fall and tremble, for their hopes will be dashed.

f.g: What they relied on (Tyre) will fail them.

chapters.n: Foreigners of mixed descent will live in Ashdod, and Philistine pride will be cut off.

f.g: A mixed or foreign people — Ashdod’s native population would be replaced.

chapters.n: God will remove the bloody, unclean food from Philistia’s mouth, and a remnant will belong to God, absorbed into Judah like the Jebusites of Jerusalem. Even enemies can be converted.

f.w: his abominations from between his teeth
f.g: Unclean, idolatrous sacrificial food.

chapters.n: God will camp around His house like a guard, so no oppressor will overrun His people again. He is watching.

f.w: I will encamp about mine house

chapters.n: A famous messianic prophecy: Zion’s King comes righteous and bringing salvation, humble and riding on a donkey’s colt. Jesus fulfilled this at His triumphal entry into Jerusalem.

f.w: behold, thy King cometh unto thee

f.g: A donkey, the mount of peace, rather than a warhorse — fitting for the Prince of Peace.

chapters.n: This King will end war, removing chariots, warhorses, and bows. He will speak peace to the nations and rule from sea to sea, to the ends of the earth.

f.w: he shall speak peace unto the heathen

chapters.n: Because of the blood of the covenant, God frees prisoners from a waterless pit. Jesus spoke of His “blood of the new testament [covenant]” at the Last Supper.

f.w: the pit wherein is no water

chapters.n: Return to the stronghold, “prisoners of hope”! God promises to restore double what was lost.

f.g: Captives who hold onto hope — a beautiful phrase for God’s people in trial.

f.w: I will render double unto thee

chapters.n: God will use Judah and Ephraim as His bow and arrow against Greece. Many see here the later Jewish struggles against Greek rulers (the Maccabees, about 167 BC).

f.g: Hebrew Yavan — Greece or Ionia.

chapters.n: The Lord will appear over His people; His arrows will flash like lightning. He will sound the trumpet and march in the southern storms.

f.w: his arrow shall go forth as the lightning

chapters.n: The Lord will defend them. They will triumph and celebrate noisily, filled like the sacrificial bowls that caught blood at the altar’s corners.
On that day God will save His people like a shepherd saves his flock. They will sparkle like jewels in a crown on His land.

f.w: as the flock of his people

chapters.n: How good and beautiful He is! Grain and new wine will make young men and women flourish — a picture of abundant blessing.

f.g: Grain.

chapters.n: Ask the Lord — not idols — for rain in spring. He makes storm clouds and gives showers and green fields. Baal was supposed to be the storm god; Zechariah insists the true source is the Lord.

f.g: Spring rains (March–April) that ripen the crops.

chapters.n: Household idols speak nonsense, fortune-tellers see lies and tell false dreams. So the people wander like sheep without a shepherd.

f.g: Hebrew teraphim — household gods used for divination.

chapters.n: God is angry with the bad shepherds (leaders) and will punish the “goats” — the strong who abuse the flock. He will turn Judah into His proud warhorse.

f.g: Leaders or bullies among the flock.

chapters.n: From Judah will come the cornerstone, the tent peg, the battle bow, and every ruler. Many see the Messiah in the cornerstone and the peg — a sure support.

f.g: Cornerstone.
A tent peg — something firm to hang everything on.

chapters.n: Judah will be like mighty warriors trampling enemies, fighting because the Lord is with them.

f.w: because the LORD is with them

chapters.n: God will strengthen Judah and save Joseph’s house (the northern tribes). He will bring them back as if He had never rejected them. Both kingdoms will be reunited.

f.g: The northern tribes, led by Ephraim and Manasseh.

f.w: as though I had not cast them off

chapters.n: Ephraim will be strong and joyful, and their children will see it and rejoice in the Lord.
God will whistle for His people and gather them, for He has redeemed them, and they will multiply as before. A shepherd’s whistle calls the flock home.

f.g: Whistle — a signal to gather.

chapters.n: God scattered Israel among the nations like seed, but in faraway lands they will remember Him, survive with their children, and return. Scattering becomes sowing.

f.w: I will sow them among the people
they shall remember me in far countries

chapters.n: God will bring them back from Egypt and Assyria, filling Gilead and Lebanon until there’s no room left.

f.w: place shall not be found for them

chapters.n: As at the Exodus, God will pass through the sea of trouble, strike the waves, and dry up the Nile. Assyria’s pride and Egypt’s rule will fall.

f.w: shall smite the waves in the sea

chapters.n: God will strengthen them, and they will walk in His name. Their strength and identity come from Him.

f.w: they shall walk up and down in his name

chapters.n: A sudden lament: Lebanon, open your gates so fire can burn your cedars. Mighty trees often symbolize proud leaders and nations.

f.g: Famous for its tall cedars.

chapters.n: Wail, cypress, for the cedar has fallen! Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the dense forest is cut down. If the greatest fall, who is safe?

f.g: Cypress or juniper.
Better: “the impenetrable forest.”

chapters.n: Hear the shepherds wailing, their glory ruined; the lions roaring, their thickets along the Jordan destroyed.

f.g: The dense thickets along the Jordan River, where lions lived (Jeremiah 49:19).

chapters.n: The Lord commands Zechariah to act out a parable: shepherd a flock doomed to slaughter. He represents God as shepherd of His people.

f.g: Sheep destined to be killed — Israel under exploitative rulers.

chapters.n: The buyers kill the sheep without guilt; the sellers say, “Praise the Lord, I’m rich!” Their own shepherds feel no pity. A picture of greedy, heartless leaders.

f.w: Blessed be the LORD; for I am rich

chapters.n: God says He will no longer spare the people of the land; He will hand them over to their neighbors and rulers.

f.g: Because they rejected His shepherding.

chapters.n: Zechariah shepherds the flock, especially the oppressed. He takes two staffs, naming them Beauty (or Favor) and Bands (or Union).

f.g: Hebrew no‘am — “favor” or “grace.”
Hebrew ḥovlim — “union” or “bonds.”

chapters.n: In one month he removes three shepherds. He grew weary of them, and the flock detested him. The identity of the three is debated.

f.g: Unclear; perhaps three leaders or classes of leaders (kings, priests, prophets).

chapters.n: The shepherd gives up: “I won’t shepherd you. Let the dying die and the rest devour each other.” Rejecting the Good Shepherd leaves people to their own destruction.

f.g: I will no longer shepherd you.

chapters.n: He breaks the staff called Beauty, symbolizing the end of God’s protective covenant with the nations around Israel.

f.g: His agreement restraining the nations from harming Israel.

chapters.n: The covenant was broken that day, and the humble sheep who were watching understood this was the Lord’s word.

f.g: The afflicted sheep — the faithful few who were paying attention.

chapters.n: The shepherd asks for his wages, and they weigh out thirty pieces of silver — the price of a slave gored by an ox. An insult to the shepherd, and to God.

The Lord says, sarcastically, “Throw it to the potter — that ‘magnificent’ price they valued me at!” Zechariah throws the silver into the temple to the potter. Matthew sees this fulfilled when Judas threw his silver into the temple and it bought a potter’s field.

f.w: a goodly price that I was prised at of them
f.g: Bitter irony: “What a fine price they thought I was worth!”

chapters.n: He breaks the second staff, Bands, ending the brotherhood between Judah and Israel — the people are divided.

f.w: the brotherhood between Judah and Israel

chapters.n: Next the Lord tells Zechariah to take the gear of a foolish, worthless shepherd.

f.g: A worthless or wicked leader.

chapters.n: Because they rejected the good shepherd, God will allow a bad one who doesn’t care for the lost, young, injured, or weak — but devours the best of the flock. The opposite of Christ, the Good Shepherd.

f.w: neither shall seek the young one, nor heal that that is broken

chapters.n: Woe to the worthless shepherd who abandons the flock! His arm will wither and his right eye go blind — the very strength and sight he should have used to protect them.

f.g: Worthless shepherd — as empty as an idol.

chapters.n: The final oracle (chapters 12–14) begins. It comes from the Creator who stretched out the heavens, founded the earth, and formed the human spirit. Latter-day Saints see much of these chapters fulfilled at the Lord’s Second Coming.

f.w: formeth the spirit of man within him

chapters.n: Jerusalem will be like a cup that makes attacking nations stagger as if drunk, when they besiege Judah and Jerusalem.

f.g: A cup that makes one reel — a symbol of God’s judgment.

chapters.n: Jerusalem will be like a heavy stone that injures anyone who tries to lift it, even if all nations unite against it.

f.g: A massive stone, perhaps like those used in ancient weightlifting contests.

f.w: all the people of the earth be gathered together against it

chapters.n: God will strike the attackers’ horses with panic and blindness and the riders with madness, while watching over Judah.

f.w: I will open mine eyes upon the house of Judah

chapters.n: Judah’s leaders will recognize that Jerusalem’s strength comes from the Lord.

f.w: my strength in the LORD of hosts

chapters.n: Judah’s leaders will be like a firepot in a woodpile or a torch among sheaves, consuming the enemies around them. Jerusalem will stand secure in its place.

f.w: an hearth of fire among the wood

chapters.n: The Lord will save the countryside of Judah first, so the royal house and Jerusalem don’t boast over the rest. God guards against pride.

f.g: The villages and countryside, outside the walled city.

chapters.n: God will protect Jerusalem so that the weakest will be as strong as David, and David’s house like God, like the angel of the Lord leading them.

f.w: he that is feeble among them at that day shall be as David
as the angel of the LORD before them

chapters.n: On that day God will destroy all the nations that attack Jerusalem.

f.w: I will seek to destroy all the nations

chapters.n: A profound prophecy: God will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer, and Jerusalem “shall look upon me whom they have pierced,” mourning as for an only child. John saw this fulfilled at the cross, and the D&C describes Jews recognizing Jesus at His coming.

f.w: they shall look upon me whom they have pierced
the spirit of grace and of supplications
as one mourneth for his only son

chapters.n: The mourning will be like the national grief at Megiddo — perhaps recalling the death of good King Josiah there.

f.g: A place near Megiddo; or possibly a pagan mourning ritual.

chapters.n: Every family will mourn separately, men and women apart — the royal family of David and of his son Nathan.
The priestly family of Levi and of his grandson Shimei will mourn too. Royal and priestly lines alike repent.
All the remaining families will mourn privately. Real repentance is personal, not just a public show.

f.g: Each in private — deep, individual sorrow.

chapters.n: A fountain will be opened to cleanse David’s house and Jerusalem from sin and impurity. Christians see this fountain in the cleansing power of Christ’s Atonement.
God will wipe out the very names of idols, so they are forgotten, and remove false prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.

f.w: cut off the names of the idols

f.g: Here, false prophets.

chapters.n: False prophecy will be so detested that even a false prophet’s own parents will condemn him, as the law of Moses required.

f.w: thou speakest lies in the name of the LORD

chapters.n: False prophets will be ashamed of their visions and stop wearing the hairy cloak prophets wore, which they used to deceive.

f.g: A hairy mantle, like Elijah’s (2 Kings 1:8).

chapters.n: Each will deny being a prophet: “I’m just a farmer; I’ve worked the land since I was young.”

f.g: Farmer.

chapters.n: Someone asks, “What are these wounds on your hands?” He answers, “I got them in my friends’ house.” In context about a false prophet, but the D&C uses similar words of Jesus showing His wounds to the Jews at His coming.

f.w: What are these wounds in thine hands?
in the house of my friends
f.g: Among those who should have loved me.

chapters.n: “Awake, sword, against my Shepherd, the man who is my companion!” Strike the Shepherd and the sheep scatter. Jesus quoted this the night of His arrest, applying it to Himself and His disciples.

f.w: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered
the man that is my fellow
f.g: My close associate — one who stands beside God, an exalted description.

chapters.n: In the land, two-thirds will be cut off and die, but one-third will remain.

God will refine the surviving third like silver and test them like gold. They will call on Him and He will answer: “They are My people,” and they will say, “The Lord is my God.” Trials purify and bind us to God.

f.w: will refine them as silver is refined

chapters.n: The day of the Lord is coming. Jerusalem will be plundered, and the loot divided right in its streets.

God will allow all nations to attack Jerusalem. The city will be captured and suffer terribly; half will go into exile, but a remnant will stay. Latter-day Saints associate this with the battle of Armageddon before Christ’s coming.

f.w: I will gather all nations against Jerusalem

chapters.n: Then the Lord Himself will go out and fight those nations, as He fought for Israel in the past.

f.w: as when he fought in the day of battle

chapters.n: His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, and it will split in two, creating a great valley. Modern revelation confirms this will happen at the Savior’s Second Coming. Jesus ascended from this mountain, and angels promised He would return the same way.

f.w: his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives

chapters.n: People will flee through the new valley as they fled the earthquake in King Uzziah’s day. Then the Lord will come with all His holy ones.

f.w: the earthquake in the days of Uzziah

f.g: An unknown place, perhaps near Jerusalem.

chapters.n: On that day the light will be strange — neither clear nor dark.

f.w: the light shall not be clear
f.g: Perhaps “there will be no cold or frost” — the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: It will be a unique day known only to the Lord, neither day nor night — and at evening there will be light. Hope dawns when it seems darkest.

f.w: which shall be known to the LORD
at evening time it shall be light

chapters.n: Living water will flow from Jerusalem, half to the Dead Sea and half to the Mediterranean, year-round. Ezekiel and Joel saw the same healing river.

f.w: living waters shall go out from Jerusalem

f.g: The eastern sea — the Dead Sea.
The western sea — the Mediterranean.

chapters.n: The Lord will be King over all the earth — one Lord, with one name. This is the Millennium, when Christ reigns personally.

f.w: the LORD shall be king over all the earth
one LORD, and his name one

chapters.n: The land around Jerusalem will become a plain, while Jerusalem is lifted high and fully inhabited, from gate to gate.

f.g: From the northern to the southern edge of Judah.

chapters.n: People will live there safely; never again will it be devoted to destruction.

f.g: No more curse or ban (Hebrew ḥerem).

chapters.n: A terrible plague will strike those who fought Jerusalem: their flesh, eyes, and tongues will rot while they stand.
The Lord will send panic among the enemies, so they turn on each other.

f.w: his hand shall rise up against the hand of his neighbour

chapters.n: Judah will also fight at Jerusalem, and the wealth of the nations — gold, silver, clothing — will be collected in abundance.

f.w: the wealth of all the heathen

chapters.n: The same plague will strike the enemy’s horses, mules, camels, donkeys, and all their animals.

f.g: The same plague described in verse 12.

chapters.n: Survivors from the hostile nations will go to Jerusalem every year to worship the King and celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles. Former enemies become worshipers.
Any nation that refuses to come worship the King will receive no rain.

f.w: upon them shall be no rain

chapters.n: Even Egypt, which depended on the Nile rather than rain, will be struck with plague if it refuses.

f.g: Egypt relied on the Nile, not rainfall, so it receives a plague instead.

chapters.n: This will be the punishment for Egypt and every nation that won’t come to keep the feast.

f.g: Literally “the sin” — the consequence of the sin.

chapters.n: In that day even horses’ bells will be engraved “Holiness unto the Lord” — the words once on the high priest’s headpiece. Ordinary cooking pots will be as sacred as altar bowls. Everything will be holy. Latter-day Saints see these words inscribed on temples today.

f.g: Sacred basins used in temple sacrifices.

chapters.n: Every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy, usable for sacred meals, and no trader will be found in the Lord’s house. Jesus cleansed the temple of merchants, foreshadowing this.

f.g: Here meaning “trader” or “merchant.”

f.w: no more the Canaanite in the house of the LORD

f.g: Boil, cook.
